report.source_text: Brain MRI including angiographic and gadolinium enhanced sequences, performed 4 months after the ophthalmic zoster infection, demonstrated the presence of subacute ischaemic changes in the right basal ganglia and the right cerebral peduncle. Narrowing of the supraclinoid segment of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) and the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and gadolinium enhancement in the vessel wall of the right ICA and ACA were noted (figure 1).

report.source_text: Treatment with natalizumab was paused. The patient was asymptomatic during in-hospital stay and discharged home after 7 days. Acyclovir was administered intravenously until the follow-up lumbar puncture, when VZV-PCR DNA was negative. Virological and microbiological analyses as above were still negative. In serum, HbsAg, anti-HCV, HIV antibodies and antigen, Treponema pallidum and VZV IgM were negative. VZV IgG was positive, as before. The ratio of CD4+/CD8+ (2.65) as well as CD4 percentage (47%) and count (0.69 x 109 /L) were normal in whole blood.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A woman in her 30s with relapsing-remitting MS on natalizumab (6 years, 56 treatments) presented with new-onset daily bilateral headache with pounding and pressing quality, evolving into right-sided occipital and retroorbital pain, accompanied by photophobia, phonophobia, and isolated right cheek twitches. Physical examination revealed hyper-reflexia in the left arm. This presentation occurred approximately 2 months after a documented right ophthalmic zoster infection. MRI brain performed 4 months post-zoster demonstrated subacute ischemic changes in the right basal ganglia and cerebral peduncle, with narrowing of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) supraclinoid segment and A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), plus gadolinium enhancement in the vessel walls of both vessels. Lumbar puncture revealed positive VZV-DNA in cerebrospinal fluid with normal cell counts, glucose, lactate, and albumin levels, confirming CNS VZV infection. The patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days, then oral prednisolone taper), intravenous acyclovir (750 mg three times daily), and acetylsalicylic acid (75 mg daily). Natalizumab was paused. The patient became asymptomatic during hospitalization and was discharged after 7 days. Follow-up lumbar puncture at 17 days post-admission showed negative VZV-PCR with normal immunological parameters. Follow-up MRI at 6 weeks post-initial MRI demonstrated persisting vasculitic vessel wall changes with gadolinium enhancement. A final follow-up MRI at 9 months showed regression of gadolinium enhancement but persisting vessel wall thickening in the affected segments with no new lesions.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: While initial presentation included migraine-like features (photophobia, phonophobia, pounding headache), the imaging findings of vasculitis with vessel narrowing, ischemic changes, and gadolinium enhancement, combined with positive VZV-DNA in CSF, definitively establish vasculopathy rather than primary migraine

Although patient has RRMS, the specific constellation of findings—recent zoster, vasculitic changes on imaging, positive VZV-DNA in CSF, and vessel wall enhancement—are characteristic of VZV vasculopathy rather than demyelinating disease
CSF analysis showed normal white cell count, normal glucose and lactate, and negative broad microbiological assay; VZV-DNA was specifically positive, ruling out other infectious etiologies
